passage:
January 1st: Kalyani wrote in big letters on the first page of her diary: THIS YEAR I WILL BE GOOD AT MATHS. She drew three stars around it.
February: Her maths marks were the same as before, 11 out of 25. She looked at the stars and felt silly. "I tried," she told Ritu didi. "What did you actually do?" Ritu asked. Kalyani couldn't think of anything.
March: Ritu helped her write something new on a sticky note: "Five sums after tea. Tick the box." Kalyani stuck it on the fridge. Every day after tea she did five sums, then ticked a box. By the end of March there were twenty-six ticks, and her unit test said 17 out of 25.

qa.q: What did the sticky note on the fridge say?
qa.a: "Five sums after tea. Tick the box."

qa.q: Why did Kalyani feel silly looking at the stars in February?
qa.a: She had made a big promise but her marks hadn't changed, and she realised she hadn't actually done anything specific.

qa.q: Why did 'five sums after tea' work when the big promise didn't?
qa.a: It was small, clear and at a set time, so it was easy to start each day and easy to check with a tick.

qa.q: How might Ritu didi feel seeing twenty-six ticks on the fridge?
qa.a: Ritu didi may feel proud that her question, 'What did you actually do?', helped Kalyani find a plan that worked 😊.

grounding: Over three months, a girl's vague vow to be good at maths does nothing until she sets five sums after tea.

passage: Jahnavi, every new year you say you'll "get better at maths", na? Your Akash dadu used to say exactly that. When I was nine, in Cuttack, I promised my mother every Sunday: "This week I'll study hard." And every Sunday I had done nothing, because what does "study hard" even mean at nine? My marks stayed at the bottom. Then our maths teacher, Pattnaik sir, gave me a different kind of promise. "Akash, after your evening milk, do five sums from page thirty. Only five. Show me on Monday." Five! I could do five. I did them every evening, then five more from page thirty-one. By the end of term I was in the middle of the class. Not the top, mind you. But the middle felt like a mountain.

qa.q: What did Pattnaik sir tell Akash to do after his evening milk?
qa.a: Do five sums from page thirty, only five, and show them on Monday.

qa.q: Why did young Akash do nothing after promising to 'study hard'?
qa.a: The promise was vague, so young Akash felt lost about where to begin, and each week slipped by with no clear step to take.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try this year instead of promising to 'get better at maths'?
qa.a: Jahnavi could set a small, specific goal, like five sums at a fixed time each day, which is easy to start and to check.

qa.q: How might Akash's mother have felt about the Sunday promises?
qa.a: She may have felt hopeful each Sunday and disappointed each week, without knowing the promise itself had no clear step in it.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how vague promises to study hard did nothing until a teacher set five sums after his evening milk.

passage: Swati's family lived in one room in a crowded Mumbai lane, and in the evenings it was loud: the TV next door, her little brother Yogesh singing, the pressure cooker whistling. For weeks she had been telling herself, "I have to get better at maths," but every evening the noise won, and she did nothing. With the half-yearly exam three weeks away, she tried something new. She wrote on the wall calendar: "After tea: 5 problems." Only five. She took her notebook to the steps outside, where it was quieter, and finished five before the streetlight came on. Yogesh came to count them with her. On the calendar she drew a small tick each day. After two weeks, the fractions that used to scare her looked almost ordinary.

qa.q: What did Swati write on the wall calendar?
qa.a: "After tea: 5 problems."

qa.q: Why did 'I have to get better at maths' lead to nothing for weeks?
qa.a: It was a big, vague wish with no starting point, so on each noisy evening Swati felt stuck and it was easy to put off.

qa.q: Which choices helped Swati follow through despite the noise?
qa.a: She set a small, specific target at a fixed time, moved to the quieter steps and ticked each day, which made starting easy and progress visible.

qa.q: What might counting the problems with Swati mean for Yogesh?
qa.a: Yogesh gets to be part of his sister's effort, which may make him proud and gives Swati a small, cheerful audience.

grounding: In a noisy one-room home with an exam near, a girl turns a vague vow into five problems after tea.

passage:
In their flat in Shillong, Damini wrote on the first page of her rough notebook: I WILL BE BETTER AT MATHS. She underlined it three times.
For two weeks nothing happened. Every evening she thought about being better at maths, then played carrom with Lalremsiami from the next flat.
After the test (9 out of 25), Lalremsiami said, 'Better how? Like, what do you actually do?'
Damini didn't know.
So they made a rule and wrote it on a sticky note on the fridge: 5 SUMS AFTER TEA. Then carrom.
The first evening, five sums took twenty minutes. By Friday they took twelve. Every day Damini put a tick on the note. When the next test came, she got 17, and there were fourteen ticks on the fridge.

qa.q: What was written on the sticky note on the fridge?
qa.a: 5 SUMS AFTER TEA.

qa.q: Why did nothing happen for two weeks after Damini wrote 'I will be better at maths'?
qa.a: Writing the wish made Damini feel hopeful, but it gave her nothing to actually do each evening, so she thought about it and then played carrom.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did the new goal work?
qa.a: Lalremsiami's question, 'What do you actually do?'; five sums after tea was small, easy to start and easy to tick, so Damini could see progress.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel seeing fourteen ticks on the fridge?
qa.a: Lalremsiami would likely feel proud of helping, since one simple question turned Damini's big wish into something she could do every day. 🙂

grounding: A child's vague vow to do better at maths goes nowhere until it becomes five sums after tea, a small goal she can start and check.

passage:
'This time I'm really going to get better at Hindi,' Aditi announced at dinner.
'You said that last term,' Ishita didi said, tearing her roti.
'This time I mean it.'
'Okay. What will you do tomorrow?'
Aditi blinked. 'Get better.'
'That's not something you do. That's a wish.' Ishita pointed at the Hindi book on the shelf. 'How about this: read one page aloud to me every night after dinner, and write down two new words.'
'Only one page?'
'One page. Every night. I'll tick it.'
The next evening Aditi appeared with the book before Ishita had finished eating. 'One page. Listen.' She stumbled on 'prashansa' and wrote it down.
'That's one,' Ishita said, and drew the first tick on the calendar.

qa.q: Which word did Aditi stumble on and write down?
qa.a: 'Prashansa'.

qa.q: Why did Aditi blink when asked what she would do tomorrow?
qa.a: Aditi was surprised and a little confused, realising she had no actual plan; 'get better' felt like a goal but gave her nothing concrete to start with.

qa.q: What turned Aditi's wish into something she could act on?
qa.a: Ishita's specific target, one page read aloud and two new words every night, ticked on the calendar; small and checkable, so Aditi started the very next evening.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Aditi turns up with the book before dinner is finished?
qa.a: Ishita probably feels pleased and a bit amused that the plan is working, and glad to be part of her sister's progress.

grounding: A child's vague promise to get better at Hindi becomes a specific nightly target that is easy to start and check.

passage: Devika, every night you promise you'll 'do better at maths', and every morning nothing changes. Your Madhuri Nani did the same, long ago. When I was ten, in our house in Nashik, I told my father every Sunday, 'This week I'll be good at maths.' And every week I wasn't. I didn't know where to start, so I didn't start. One Sunday my father said, 'Madhuri, "good at maths" is a mountain. Nobody climbs a mountain. You climb one step.' He tore a page from the calendar and wrote on it: five sums, after tea, every day. Then he stuck it on the wall. Five sums was nothing. I could finish them before my tea went cold, and each day I ticked the box. By the end of the month I had thirty ticks, and I actually understood long division.

qa.q: What did Madhuri's father write on the calendar page?
qa.a: He wrote: five sums, after tea, every day.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri never start when she promised to be 'good at maths'?
qa.a: The wish was so big and vague that she felt lost about where to begin, so nothing happened.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made progress possible?
qa.a: Her father turning the vague wish into a specific daily target, five sums after tea, that was easy to start and to check.

qa.q: How might her father have felt seeing thirty ticks?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud and pleased that his small plan helped her understand long division.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how her vague vow to be good at maths went nowhere until it became five sums after tea.

passage: All summer, Chandrika's grandmother and three cousins were staying in their two-room house in Madurai, and there was never a quiet corner. 'I'll get better at maths this holiday,' Chandrika kept saying. By July she hadn't opened her maths book once. There was always noise, always something. Her mother, Vinita, found her sulking on the step. 'What does "better" mean?' Chandrika shrugged. 'Better.' 'How about five sums, right after your bath, on the terrace, before the cousins wake up?' 'Just five?' 'Just five. And you tick the calendar.' The next morning Chandrika did five sums on the terrace while a crow watched. She ticked the calendar. By the end of the holiday there were twenty-eight ticks, and she had finished the whole chapter on decimals.

qa.q: Where did Chandrika do her five sums?
qa.a: She did them on the terrace, right after her bath.

qa.q: Why had Chandrika not opened her maths book by July?
qa.a: Her wish to 'get better' was vague, and in a noisy house she felt stuck, with no clear place to start.

qa.q: What made Vinita's suggestion work?
qa.a: It set a small, specific target, five sums at a set time and place, with a tick to check, which was easy to start even in a busy house.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel seeing twenty-eight ticks?
qa.a: Vinita would likely feel pleased and proud that a small plan helped her daughter finish the decimals chapter.

grounding: In a crowded house, a child's vague wish to improve at maths goes nowhere until it becomes five sums after her bath.

passage: Every time Suraj got a maths test back, he made a speech in their Salt Lake flat. 'From tomorrow I'm going to be amazing at maths.' His sister Kalyani had heard it four times. Nothing changed; the speeches were the only thing that happened. After the fifth speech, Kalyani took a sticky note and wrote: 5 problems. After tea. Then tick. She stuck it on the fridge above the tea tin. 'That's it?' Suraj said. 'Five?' 'Five. Every day. Tick when done.' The next day, after tea, he did five fraction problems in fifteen minutes and ticked the note with a flourish. By the end of the week he had filled the sticky note with ticks and asked for a new one. He hadn't made a single speech.

qa.a: She stuck it on the fridge above the tea tin.

qa.q: Why did Suraj's speeches not change anything?
qa.a: The promise to be 'amazing at maths' felt big and exciting but vague, so he never knew what to actually do the next day.

qa.q: Why did the sticky note work?
qa.a: It set a small, specific goal, five problems after tea, with a tick to check, which made starting easy and progress visible.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel when Suraj asks for a new note?
qa.a: Kalyani would likely feel pleased and a little amused that her simple note worked better than all his speeches.

grounding: A child's grand vows to be amazing at maths change nothing until his sister turns them into five problems after tea.

passage:
“Suraj Bhaiya, I'm going to be better at maths this year.”
“Great. How?”
“Just… better. I'll work harder.”
Two weeks later.
“Santosh, how's the ‘better at maths’?”
“Bad. I got 9 in the class test.”
“Did you practise?”
“I meant to. Every day I say ‘today I'll do maths’, and then it's night.”
“Okay. Try this. After tea, five problems. Only five. From the exercise at the back.”
“Only five?”
“Five. Then tick them off on this paper.”
A week later, Santosh ran in waving the paper. “Look! Seven days, seven ticks! Thirty-five problems!”
“And?”
“And I understood the multiplying thing. The one with the zeroes.”
Suraj grinned. “See? ‘Better’ is hard to start. ‘Five after tea’ is easy.”

qa.q: How many problems did Santosh do in a week?
qa.a: He did thirty-five problems, five a day for seven days.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when he ran in waving the paper?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, because he could see seven ticks and had finally understood the multiplying with zeroes.

qa.q: Why did “five problems after tea” work when “better at maths” didn't?
qa.a: A specific small goal was easy to start and easy to check, unlike a vague wish.

qa.q: How might Suraj Bhaiya feel seeing the seven ticks?
qa.a: Suraj Bhaiya likely feels pleased and proud that his simple idea helped his little brother.

grounding: The dialogue shows a child whose vague vow to improve at maths goes nowhere until he sets a specific target of five problems after tea.

passage:
At the start of Class 5, I promised to get good at maths. I wrote “MATHS!!” on my bedroom wall in pencil.
Nothing happened. For a month I felt guilty every time I saw it.
My friend Ujjwal is good at maths. I asked him how he did it. He said, “I do five sums every day after tea. Then I play.”
Five sums? That's all?
So I tried. After tea, five sums from the book. I drew a small box on the wall under “MATHS!!” and ticked it each day.
Some days it took ten minutes, some days half an hour. But I always knew when I was done.
After a month, there were thirty ticks. In the next test I got 16 out of 25. Last time it was 8. I, Harish, think five is a very good number.

qa.q: What did Harish write on the bedroom wall?
qa.a: Harish wrote “MATHS!!” in pencil.

qa.q: How did Harish feel during the first month of the vague promise?
qa.a: Harish felt guilty every time Harish saw the word, because nothing had actually been started.

qa.q: What made Ujjwal's advice work for Harish?
qa.a: It gave a small, specific target, five sums after tea, that was easy to start and to tick off.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel if he heard about the 16 out of 25?
qa.a: Ujjwal might feel happy and proud that his simple routine helped a friend.

grounding: The account shows a child whose vague vow to get good at maths goes nowhere until a specific daily target of five sums.

passage:
Tuition teacher's note, Class 4, Saturday.
For three weeks, Vaibhav has told me, “I will do better in maths, Ma'am. I promise.” Each week, no homework was done. He is sincere, but the promise has nothing in it he can start.
Today his grandfather, Mr Jagdish Rao, came to collect him and mentioned they have tea at 5 every evening.
So we tried something small. I wrote on a card: “After 5 o'clock tea: 5 problems from page 42. Tick when done.” Vaibhav read it aloud and said, “Only five? That's easy.”
His grandfather agreed to sit with him and check the ticks. I asked Vaibhav to bring the card next Saturday.
What I will do next: check the card with him, praise each tick, and if all seven days are done, move him to page 43.

qa.q: What was written on the card?
qa.a: “After 5 o'clock tea: 5 problems from page 42. Tick when done.”

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when he read the card aloud?
qa.a: He felt relieved and confident, saying “Only five? That's easy,” instead of feeling stuck with a big promise.

qa.q: Why is the card more useful than Vaibhav's promise?
qa.a: It gives a specific small goal with a set time, which is easier to start and to check than a vague wish.

qa.q: How might Mr Jagdish Rao feel about helping with the ticks?
qa.a: He might feel pleased and involved, glad to have a simple way to support his grandson.

grounding: The tuition teacher's note shows a child's vague promise to improve at maths turned into a specific target of five problems after tea.

passage: Monsoon rain kept Mohit indoors all week in the village, and every day he told his grandfather, "I'm going to get better at maths this holiday." Every day, he didn't open the book. On Friday, Jatin Dadu set down his tea. "Better is too big a word. Let's make it small. After your evening tea, five sums. Only five. Then you can go and watch the rain." Mohit frowned. "Only five?" "Only five. Every day." That evening, after tea, Mohit did five sums on his slate. He showed Dadu, who drew a small star on the wall with chalk. The next day, another five, another star. By the end of the monsoon, there were twenty stars on the wall, and Mohit was faster at subtraction than his cousin.

qa.q: How many stars were on the wall by the end of the monsoon?
qa.a: Twenty stars.

qa.q: Why did Mohit never open the book when his goal was "better at maths"?
qa.a: The goal felt too big and vague, so Mohit didn't know where to start and felt stuck.

qa.q: What did Jatin Dadu do that helped?
qa.a: He turned the vague wish into a small, specific target, five sums after evening tea, with a chalk star to check it.

qa.q: How might Jatin Dadu feel seeing the twenty stars?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud and pleased with his grandson's steady work.

grounding: In the monsoon a boy vows to get better at maths and does nothing until his grandfather makes it five sums after tea.

passage: During the Christmas holidays in Madrid, Javier told his neighbour Anders, "This year I'm going to be good at maths." He said it on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. He didn't do a single problem. On Thursday, Anders, who was twelve and very organised, asked, "What does 'good at maths' mean? When will you do it?" Javier shrugged. "Just... better." Anders pulled out a notebook. "Five problems after your merienda. Every day. I'll check." Javier rolled his eyes. But that afternoon, after his bread and chocolate, he did five problems. It took twenty minutes. Anders ticked the page. The next day, five more. By Twelfth Night, Javier had done fifty problems and understood fractions. "Better," he said, "turns out to mean five a day."

qa.q: How many problems had Javier done by Twelfth Night?
qa.a: Fifty problems.

qa.q: Why did Javier do nothing for three days despite his promise?
qa.a: "Good at maths" was vague, so Javier felt unsure where to begin and never started.

qa.q: Why did Anders's plan work?
qa.a: A small, specific goal, five problems after merienda, was easy to start and easy to check with a tick.

qa.q: How might Anders feel ticking Javier's page each day?
qa.a: Anders probably felt pleased and a little proud to see his plan working.

grounding: During the Christmas holidays a boy vows to be good at maths and does nothing until a friend makes it five problems after his snack.

passage:
Every term, Rekha wrote the same line in her school diary: "I WILL get better at maths." Every term, nothing changed.
That summer the community centre on her lane ran afternoon classes to escape the heat. Bhavna Didi, who ran them, read the diary line and tapped it. "Better how? When?"
Rekha shrugged. "Just... better."
"Try this. Five sums, every day, right after tea, at this table. Then tick a box." She drew thirty little boxes on a card.
The first week Rekha grumbled. But five was small enough to start, and after tea was easy to remember. By the end of the month the card had twenty-six ticks, and in the centre's small test she got eight out of ten, her best ever. She drew a new card herself.

qa.q: How many boxes did Bhavna Didi draw on the card?
qa.a: Thirty.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when she drew the new card herself?
qa.a: Rekha felt proud and motivated; the ticks and her best-ever test showed real progress, so she wanted to keep going. 🎉

qa.q: Why did five sums after tea work where "I WILL get better" didn't?
qa.a: A small, specific goal tied to a set time is easy to start and easy to check, while "better" has no first step.

qa.q: How might Bhavna Didi see Rekha's old diary line?
qa.a: She likely sees a real wish with no plan behind it, which is why she asked, "Better how? When?"

grounding: A child who keeps vowing to do better at maths makes progress only when she commits to five sums after tea.
